briefs.headline: Share of US in India’s exports remains same
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Last year’s tariff shock by US president Donald Trump has prompted many businesses to relook their strategy of focusing on the American market, home to some of the world’s largest companies. And, govt has also sought to add to the efforts by expanding the list of countries with which India has trade agreements by adding EFTA, the UK and Oman to the list, with the European Union and Canada in the pipeline.
But 18 months since Trump announced “reciprocal tariffs” in April 2025, the share of US in India’s export basket has remained virtually unchanged, dropping from 19.8% at the end of March 2025 to 19.6% at the end of Sept 2026. Exporters of traditional items, such as garments and footwear, say the scale of the orders in US is much bigger, compared with markets such as EU. Besides, they point out that successive govts from Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s time had worked on forging strong ties with the US, until Trump upset the calculations. No wonder, the share of US in India’s exports has nearly doubled from 11% in 2009-10.
US gained share, while the EU, the UK, EFTA and the Gulf Cooperation Council lost out. 
For instance, EU accounted for 12% of India’s exports in 2009-10 -- higher than the US -- which dropped to 9.5% by FY2020 and to 8.4% in FY2025. And, despite the recent push, the declining trend has continued with the trading bloc’s share further dipped to 7.9% during April-Sept. Similarly, GCC’s share has been slid from 18.6% in 2009-10 to 13.5% in the first half of this fiscal year, while EFTA has dropped from 5.4% to 1.7% during this period. Oman is the sole exception, with its share almost doubling from 1.2% in FY2010 to 2.3% during April-Sept, recovering from a dip to 0.9% at the end of FY2020. But then, disruptions in West Asia has resulted in Oman becoming a gateway of sorts for UAE trade.
“Diversification is not easy,” says a footwear exporter, who has spent the past year meeting potential buyers in Europe. With tariffs here to stay, an engineering goods exporter, whose products face 50% additional tariff and who has been scouting for opportunities in Europe, has a similar story to tell although is looking to make some impact.
While some industry bodies and some exporters in private said that it may make sense for India to wait and not settle for a trade deal with 17% additional tariffs, instead of 25% in the absence of a pact, those supporting an agreement are far more. Besides, they fear that Trump may launch a further tariff offensive against countries that do not sign an agreement. Unlike China, which controls critical elements of the supply chain, the leverage for India is far limited.

briefs.headline: Trusts move HC to block chair’s casting vote at Tata Sons meet
briefs.deck: Tata Trusts have launched a legal challenge against Tata Sons concerning the chairman's casting vote, citing governance issues before a crucial board meeting. They argue that earlier resolutions breach the company’s articles and are seeking compensation. Holding a significant stake in Tata Sons, the Trusts aim to ensure their nominee directors' votes carry equal weight, reflecting the continuing…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and R D Tata Trust (RDTT) have moved Bombay high court to block the 
Tata Sons
 chairman from using his casting vote to break a potential tie on resolutions involving the Trusts’ nominee directors at the Nov 30 board meeting, escalating the governance battle over control of India’s largest conglomerate by revenue.
Trusts have also sought to invalidate 
N Chandrasekaran
’s reappointment as chairman, arguing that the process violated the company’s articles, and have claimed Rs 65 crore in damages from the company and its board, except Noel Tata, plus 18% annual interest until payment.
Senior counsel Abhishek Manu Singhvi and Janak Dwarkadas mentioned the two suits on Thursday for an urgent hearing in view of the board meeting on Monday.
Chandra set to chair board for most resolutions, giving him casting vote
Tata Trusts first approached Justice Arif Doctor for a hearing, but he recused. They then approached Justice Abhay Ahuja, who agreed to hear them on Friday.
SDTT through trustee Bhaskar Bhat and RDTT through Rishi Sharma, head of legal at Tata Trusts, have argued that Tata Sons used the chairman’s casting vote to push through a board resolution when the Trusts’ two nominee directors split, producing a tie, at the last board meeting on Sept 17. The Trusts fear the same device will be used on Nov 30 to push through resolutions including conversion of Tata Sons into a public company and its listing, amendments to its articles and an EGM on Chandrasekaran’s reappointment, while Noel’s merger proposal to avoid an IPO will be defeated.
The Trusts sought a declaration from the HC that the resolution passed on Sept 17, 2026, for Chandrasekaran’s reappointment is invalid and a direction to restrain Tata Sons from acting on the resolution on Chandrasekaran’s reappointment. Chandrasekaran’s current term expires on Feb 20, 2027.
SDTT specifically seeks to restrain Chandrasekaran or Harish Manwani or any other person acting as chairman of any meeting of the board of Tata Sons from exercising a casting vote when Trust-nominated directors differ.
At the last board meeting, according to the suits, Trusts’ nominees Noel and Venu Srinivasan voted against and in favour, respectively, on Chandrasekaran’s reappointment. Independent director Harish Manwani, who chaired that item after Chandrasekaran recused himself, used his casting vote to carry it.
Agenda for the next meeting includes confirming the Sept 17 minutes. Trusts argued such moves would render their affirmative voting rights under Article 121 ineffective. Chandrasekaran is set to chair the board for most of the resolutions, giving him the casting vote in the event of a tie. He will not chair the one on his own reappointment.
At the heart of the dispute are Articles 118 and 121 of Tata Sons’ articles of association. The Trusts argue that Article 121 requires a majority of the Trusts’ nominee directors to vote in favour of key board resolutions. With only two nominees, that means both must support a resolution, and a casting vote cannot cure a 1-1 split. The Trusts say the casting vote applies only when the whole board is tied. They also said Chandrasekaran’s reappointment should have followed Article 118, which provides for a selection committee. The Trusts cited section 10(1) of the Companies Act, which binds a company to its articles, and Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TCS v Cyrus Investments.
Tata Sons, however, argues that Article 118 applies only to the appointment of a new chairman and that Article 121 gives the chairman a casting vote when the two Trusts’ nominees’ votes are divided.
The Trusts said they decided to move court after a series of communications to Tata Sons since the Sept 17 meeting, raising objections and seeking corrective action, failed to elicit a satisfactory response. On Nov 25, the two trusts, which together hold about 30% of Tata Sons, passed by majority resolutions backing legal action against the company and its entire board, with Srinivasan and Vijay Singh voting against.

Apart from Chandrasekaran, Noel, Srinivasan and Manwani, the other Tata Sons directors are executive director and CFO Saurabh Agrawal and independent director Anita George. SDTT has sought Rs 50 crore and RDTT Rs 15 crore in damages from Tata Sons and the five directors.

briefs.headline: Venu, Vijay urge probe into SDTT’s action on Tata Sons
briefs.deck: Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh met with the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner to discuss concerns surrounding the legal actions of the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust. They highlighted potential misuse of charitable resources in lawsuits involving Tata Sons and brought forth specific requests for transparency and an inquiry into the Trust's operations. Their primary objective is to safeguard public…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Venu Srinivasan and 
Vijay Singh
, vice-chairmen of Tata Trusts, asked the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner (MCC) on Thursday to inquire into Sir Dorabji Tata Trust’s (SDTT) decision to sue 
Tata Sons
. The same day, SDTT and R D Tata Trust (RDTT) filed separate suits in the Bombay high court against Tata Sons and five of its directors, Srinivasan among them.
Srinivasan and Singh had opposed the two Trusts' Nov 25 resolutions authorising suits to invalidate N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons chairman and to bar the chairman's casting vote on board resolutions when the Trusts' two nominee directors vote differently.
They said their objection was not to SDTT defending its shareholder rights, but to the breadth of the relief sought and the use of charitable resources in litigation that could impede Tata Sons' compliance with the RBI's listing requirement.
They opposed the resolutions at both Trusts, but their MCC complaints name SDTT alone. SDTT, the flagship of Tata Trusts, owns about 28% of Tata Sons, while RDTT holds about 2%.
"A preference for keeping Tata Sons privately held, or a disagreement with the company's governance decisions, cannot by itself justify using charitable resources to frustrate an independent regulatory obligation," they said in separate but identical complaints.
They argued that if the Bombay high court granted the restraint, Tata Sons could be caught between an RBI mandate to take listing-related steps and a court order barring its board from doing so. "That would create an unacceptable regulatory and governance impasse," they said. No internal voting mechanism, they added, "can confer a veto over the regulator or create, by indirection, a stay that the regulator itself has not granted."
SDTT's position as a shareholder, they said, did not allow its trustees to treat Tata Sons "as an extension of the Trust or to subordinate the requirements of law to an internal governance contest".
Despite their opposition, the other three SDTT trustees, Noel Tata, Neville Tata and Bhaskar Bhat, carried the Nov 25 resolution.
Srinivasan and Singh asked for an inquiry before the Nov 30 Tata Sons board meeting, which is due to consider the listing. They also asked that SDTT commit no further funds to pursuing the interim restraint aimed at that meeting, and that they be heard before it.
The complaints invoked sections 37, 41A and 41B of the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, which let the commissioner call for trust records, issue directions to trustees and open an inquiry.
They demanded the full paper trail behind SDTT's decision, from individual votes and legal advice to the suits filed, litigation costs and source of funds.
They asked the commissioner to determine whether trustees saw the RBI's Sept and Nov communications, both of which told Tata Sons to comply with its rules, including the listing requirement, before approving the litigation. If necessary, they wanted the regulatory and charitable issues placed before the Bombay high court.
They said they were not asking the MCC to rule on Chandrasekaran's reappointment, which is a matter for the court. "I do not ask you to presume misconduct. I ask that these matters be examined before public charitable funds and the Trust's institutional position are exposed to consequences that may be difficult to reverse," they said.

stories.headline: Sandpapergate: Cricket Australia forum will not determine responsibility for ball tampering
stories.deck: CA announced on November 18 it would ‌open an independent forum for all the players and staff to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 ‌without fear of sanction
stories.bodyText:
Cricket Australia's (CA) forum into the ball-tampering scandal of 2018 will not determine responsibility or make adverse findings against any individual, according to its terms of reference published on Friday (November 27, 2026).
The ‌scandal was reignited this month after former Australia batter Usman Khawaja said the whole team had known about the ball-tampering plot during the tour of South Africa, not just the three players found culpable by CA's integrity unit.
CA announced on November 18 it would ‌open an independent forum for all the players and staff to give their accounts of what happened in 2018 ‌without fear of sanction.
The six-week forum, to be overseen by ‌Australian barrister Fiona McLeod, will be an "information-gathering and listening process", rather than a disciplinary process, its terms of reference said.
It will not make "any adverse findings about, or determine the responsibility of, any individual", nor revisit the sanctions previously imposed. There will be no ‌recommendations for retrospective punishment or legal action and participation will be entirely voluntary.
"Its purpose is to support the welfare of those impacted and to provide Participants with an opportunity to be heard ‌and to have their experience acknowledged and understood without fear of retribution or disadvantage," the terms said.
CA's investigation in 2018 found only three players culpable -- former captain Steve Smith and opening batters David Warner and Cameron Bancroft.
Smith and Warner were banned for 12 months, with Bancroft suspended for nine.
Khawaja's former teammates ‌Warner, Bancroft and Chadd Sayers have supported his claims that the wider playing group and staff were aware of the ball-tampering.
However, captain Pat Cummins and bowlers Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood have flatly denied any prior knowledge.
CA backed Cummins to remain captain of the test and one-day international sides last week and rejected any suggestion his ‌integrity had been compromised amid the renewed furore.
The scope of CA's forum will include "ball-management practices" by the men's team during all four tests of the South Africa tour and not just the Newlands test where Australia's ball-tampering was exposed.
It will also include the conduct and scope of CA's investigation in 2018.
CA said a report into the forum would be published in full and it ‌would respond within 30 days.
"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn," CA chairman David Boon said in a statement.

stories.headline: Cricket Australia gives players six weeks to share accounts of ball-tampering scandal
stories.deck: Cricket Australia has initiated an independent forum to delve into the controversial events of the 2018 South Africa cricket tour. This platform encourages players and staff to confidentially recount their experiences related to the ball-tampering incident. Led by senior counsel Fiona McLeod, the forum prioritizes confidentiality and aims to document findings, with reports expected to be…
stories.bodyText:
Cricket Australia (CA) has made public the terms of reference for its independent forum examining the events surrounding the controversial 2018 South Africa tour, which became infamous for the ball-tampering scandal. The six-week exercise will give players and support staff who were part of the tour an opportunity to share their experiences, although individual accounts will remain confidential and will not be made available to the CA Board.
The board will instead receive a report summarising the key issues raised during the process, along with recommendations. The document will not include individual testimonies or any supporting material. CA has also committed to releasing the complete report, together with its response, within 30 days of receiving it.
The independent exercise will be overseen by senior counsel Fiona McLeod AO SC, who will conduct private sessions with those willing to participate. The forum was announced following fresh revelations surrounding the 2018 scandal in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, 
Sabr
.
In the book, Khawaja claimed that awareness of the sandpaper plan extended beyond the three players who were sanctioned by CA. 
David Warner
 and 
Cameron Bancroft
 have supported parts of his account, while 
Pat Cummins
 and several other bowlers have maintained that they had no knowledge of the plan.
The forum will examine Australia's ball-management practices during the 2017-18 season, the team's involvement in all four Tests of the South Africa tour, and the incident involving Bancroft during the third Test in Cape Town on March 24, 2018. It will also look into CA's subsequent investigation into the episode.
However, the exercise is not intended to reopen the original investigation or establish individual responsibility for the incident.
CA has extended invitations to all players and support staff who were part of the South Africa tour, along with the management officials and board directors who were associated with the organisation at the time. Participants will be able to share their accounts through face-to-face or online meetings with McLeod, submit written statements or provide relevant documents.
Taking part in the process is voluntary, and those who choose to participate will be permitted to have a support person or legal representative present.
The terms of reference also lay down safeguards to protect the confidentiality of participants. Information shared by one individual cannot be attributed to them when seeking clarification from another participant unless they provide consent. Those involved will be informed about who can access their submissions and will have the opportunity to verify their own accounts for accuracy.
In addition, the forum will be given access to the 2018 Culture and Governance Review of Australian Cricket conducted by The Ethics Centre, along with other relevant records and documents it considers necessary.
CA Chair David Boon said the organisation was grateful to McLeod for agreeing to lead the initiative, which has been designed to provide a platform for everyone involved in the tour to share their experiences.
“We’re grateful to Fiona McLeod AO SC for agreeing to lead the Independent Forum which has been designed to give voice to all the players and staff on the 2018 Test tour of South Africa," Boon said.
“This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation.
“We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.
“This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn.
“Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn.
“It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate.”

stories.headline: World chess championship: Sindarov admits Gukesh out-prepared him in third game
stories.deck: With the scores tied at 1.5-1.5 after three consecutive draws, Sindarov acknowledged that Gukesh, who was playing with Black pieces in Game 3, had caught him off guard with his preparation in the opening
stories.bodyText:
Challenger Javokhir Sindarov admitted he was out-prepared by defending champion D Gukesh in the third game of the World Chess Championship in Geneva, as the Indian's opening preparation put the Uzbek under pressure.
With the scores tied at 1.5-1.5 after three consecutive draws, Sindarov acknowledged that Gukesh, who was playing with Black pieces in Game 3, had caught him off guard with his preparation in the opening.
"Today my opponent was really well prepared. We checked this move 5...Be7, but not that deep. I was surprised. I thought I got a very good position, but my opponent was really well prepared.
"I was just trying to find some chances because I was playing as White. In the endgame, I started to understand that the position was completely equal, and in the time trouble I was really very close to missing something. But I'm happy that I defended very well”, Sindarov said in the post game press conference.
For the first time in the match, Gukesh was seen blitzing out his opening moves while Sindarov, playing with White, remained glued to his chair, spending considerable time trying to navigate the position.
"I knew the position was already pretty much equal, but it's still a little bit of an ugly structure for Black. So I knew it would be a game, but I felt pretty comfortable in the sense that I had a lot more time, and I knew some of the plans in this structure," noted Gukesh.
The Indian said he was comfortable with the position but acknowledged that Sindarov's counterplay briefly threatened to make things uncomfortable.
"My bishop is kind of offside, and my rook is on a4, it's doing a good job, but if kingside action starts, my pieces are not perfectly placed for the action. Maybe there are more options to hold, but I thought what I did was pretty important, because otherwise I felt it was getting unpleasant," Gukesh said about the counterplay his opponent found.
Sindarov admitted it had been a difficult day at the board, with Gukesh seemingly knowing his preparation until around the 15th move.
"Today, it was a little bit of a hard day for me. My opponent was really prepared very well, and I think until move 15 he knew everything. I spent a lot of time in the opening.
"Maybe I need to play some moves faster. But I'm just trying to find some chances, and maybe some other moves were better, which I saw, but still, in general, I'm happy with my game. I will try to take a rest and we'll prepare for the next game, but I'll try to enjoy the match”, the challenger said.
Gukesh, on the other hand, felt the game had been interesting despite the opening advantage not translating into a win.
"It was super interesting. After the opening, it felt like it was not going to be very interesting, but as usual with both of us, we always find some way to create chances.
"I think it was most stressful for him, because I always had enough time on the clock, so it was not too stressful for me. But it was a little stressful when he had about 7 seconds for the last move. That was stressful. But other than that, it was all good”, the Indian ace said.
Gukesh also credited his team for the opening preparation.
“I'm pretty happy with how the opening went, and a lot of credit to my team, who prepared this line”.
On the pressure of three successive draws, Sindarov said he was not thinking too much about the scores, while Gukesh felt there was still a long way to go in the 14-game contest.
“There is always pressure in every game of the match. Three draws sound like a big thing, but it's in the context of 14 games, so we're not even anywhere close to halfway. It's a long match. We are both trying, we are both playing good chess, and we are both strong opponents, so it's not easy to win a game whenever you want to," Gukesh said.
"We try to create chances and make the most out of them, but so far none of us really got too many big chances. And it's also a good thing that we're playing. It usually means that we are playing good chess. The quality is high” the world champion observed.
The match will resume after the first rest day on Friday (November 27, 2026), with the fourth game scheduled for Saturday (November 28, 2026).

stories.headline: Yashasvi Jaiswal surpasses Sachin Tendulkar to create history with rare Test feat
stories.deck: Yashasvi Jaiswal has reached an impressive milestone by competing in his 33rd Test match at a different venue, joining the ranks of Sanjay Manjrekar as one of the few players to achieve this feat. Throughout his Test career, he has faced seven distinct teams, with his journey set to advance in the anticipated Border-Gavaskar Trophy against Australia in 2027.
stories.bodyText:
Yashasvi Jaiswal
 achieved a rare milestone in Test cricket on Friday (November 27), becoming only the second player in the world to feature in each of his first 33 Test matches at different venues.
The India opener reached the landmark during the second Test against New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. Since making his international debut in the longest format against the West Indies at Windsor Park in Roseau on July 12, 2023, Jaiswal has represented India in 33 Tests, with every appearance coming at a different ground.
Former India batter 
Sanjay Manjrekar
 is the only other player to have achieved the feat, having played his first 33 Tests at 33 different venues. Legendary batter 
Sachin Tendulkar
 is next on the list, having featured in his first 32 Tests at separate grounds.
Former India fast bowler Javagal Srinath and West Indies wicketkeeper-batter Denesh Ramdin complete the top five. Both played their first 24 Test matches at different venues for their respective countries.
Most Tests at different venues from debut
Jaiswal's 33 Test appearances have come across seven opposition teams. He has played 10 matches against England, five each against New Zealand and Australia, four apiece against the West Indies and South Africa, two each against Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and one against Afghanistan.
The 24-year-old will have an opportunity to move past Manjrekar and claim the outright record when India begin their five-Test Border-Gavaskar Trophy campaign against Australia in 2027.
The opening Test of the series is scheduled to be played at the Vidarbha Cricket Association Stadium in Nagpur from January 21 to 25. Jaiswal has already made an appearance at the venue, having played his ODI debut against England there on February 6, 2025. However, he is yet to feature in a red-ball international at the ground.
A place in India's playing XI for the Nagpur Test would take Jaiswal's streak to 34 matches at different venues. However, his run is unlikely to extend beyond that, as the remaining four Tests of the series are scheduled to be held in Chennai, Guwahati, Ranchi and Ahmedabad, where he has already played Test cricket.
The other venues for the 2027 Border-Gavaskar Trophy are MA Chidambaram Stadium in Chennai, Barsapara Cricket Stadium in Guwahati, JSCA International Stadium Complex in Ranchi and Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad. Jaiswal has featured in a Test at each of these grounds, meaning an appearance in the Chennai match after the Nagpur opener would bring his streak to an end at 34.
Meanwhile, India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl against New Zealand in the second Test, which began at Hagley Oval on Friday.
India made one change to their playing XI, handing fast bowler Gurnoor Brar his Test debut in place of Prasidh Krishna. Jasprit Bumrah presented the debutant with his Test cap.
New Zealand, meanwhile, opted to retain the same playing XI from the previous Test.

briefs.headline: IND vs NZ second Test: Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj turn tables for India before tea
briefs.deck: The second session saw India picking three wickets for just 54 runs in 24 overs and will hope to capitalise in the last session
briefs.bodyText:
Akash Deep turned the tables around as the seamer’s spirited spell pegged New Zealand back and brought India back in the game in the second session of Day One brought India right into the second Test against New Zealand.
Akash and Anshul Kamboj struck thrice in 16 balls without an addition of a run before Daryl Mitchell and Tom Blundell survived a tricky period before. At tea, New Zealand was 131 for four.
Also read | IND vs NZ second Test: Morne Morkel urges patience with Anshul Kamboj’s performance
Akash, easily the pick of the bowlers since Shubman Gill chose to bowl after winning yet another toss, swung the pendulum in India’s favour in his third spell that read 7-4-7-2. He unsettled Tom Latham (59, 128b, 6x4) with his channel balls, then got him to edge a short-ball but it ricocheted off the helmet to fall safe and finally left Latham clueless with a near-perfect ball in the channel.
Kamboj, who had also kept things tight at the other end, then had Henry Nicholls pull one straight to long-leg before Akash forced Rachin Ravindra into a nick bowling around the wickets. From 110 for one, the home team was reduced to 110 for four and the home crowd, a superb turnout for a Friday on the grass banks, literally turned silent.
The second session saw India picking three wickets for just 54 runs in 24 overs and will hope to capitalise in the last session.

briefs.headline: 0 runs, 3 wickets! India bowlers produce stunning turnaround vs New Zealand
briefs.deck: India's fast bowlers made a strong comeback by taking three wickets quickly after struggling initially. Akash Deep was instrumental in breaking the New Zealand innings by dismissing Tom Latham. Anshul Kamboj contributed by sending back Henry Nicholls and Rachin Ravindra in quick succession. Despite losing three wickets, Tom Blundell faced numerous close calls from the Indian bowlers.
briefs.bodyText:
India came roaring back with a superb spell of fast bowling in the second Test against New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. After creating several chances without success, the Indian bowlers finally found their rhythm and picked up three wickets in the space of three overs.
The sudden burst put New Zealand on the back foot, with Shubman Gill's decisions paying off. Akash Deep was the star of the spell, taking two wickets, while Anshul Kamboj also made an important contribution.
Akash Deep breaks the stand, Kamboj strikes next
India were looking for a breakthrough at the drinks break after New Zealand reached 106/1 at the end of 39 overs. The visitors had come close on several occasions but had little to show for their efforts.
There were missed run-out opportunities, a DRS call that did not go their way and a few edges and top-edges that failed to bring wickets. The ball was still moving off the surface, but the Indian bowlers were unable to make the most of it.
Akash Deep eventually gave India the much-needed breakthrough in the 42nd over by dismissing New Zealand captain Tom Latham. The left-hander had made 59 off 128 deliveries before a brilliant delivery ended his stay.
Akash Deep bowled a good-length delivery outside off stump. The ball came in initially before holding its line, forcing Latham to play at it. 
He managed only a faint outside edge, which was safely collected by wicketkeeper Rishabh Pant.
The dismissal lifted the Indian team's spirits after a frustrating period in which they had struggled to break through.
India did not have to wait long for another wicket. In the following over, Anshul Kamboj sent Henry Nicholls back for 16 off 46 balls.
Kamboj bowled a short delivery, prompting Nicholls to attempt a pull shot. The batter was early into the stroke and could only manage a top edge. Akash Deep made no mistake at long leg to complete the catch.
Akash Deep then delivered another beauty to dismiss Rachin Ravindra for a duck and complete a remarkable spell for India.
Coming from around the wicket, the pacer got the ball to move in with the angle before taking it away off the seam. Ravindra went forward to defend but edged it to Pant, who took his second catch of the spell.
In the space of three overs, New Zealand had gone from 110/1 to 110/4, giving India a big opportunity to take control of the match.
Tom Blundell survives multiple close calls
Even after picking up three quick wickets, the Indian bowlers kept creating problems for the New Zealand batters. However, Tom Blundell managed to survive a series of close calls.
In the 45th over, Kamboj produced a big inswinger that struck Blundell on the pads. India appealed loudly for LBW, but Gill decided not to take a review after consulting the bowler. The delivery appeared to be going down the leg side.
Blundell had another close escape against Gurnoor Brar in the 47th over. The pacer bowled a delivery at 136 kmph that pitched on off stump before moving away sharply. It beat Blundell's outside edge and went just over the off bail.
Bumrah then thought he had Blundell trapped in front in the 48th over. After a discussion with Gill, India decided to review the umpire's decision.
The pacer bowled a delivery that came back in sharply and beat Blundell's inside edge before hitting him on the back thigh. However, the ball-tracking showed that the delivery was going over the middle stump.
India lost another review, while Blundell survived yet another testing moment against the Indian pace attack.

briefs.headline: Tom Latham overtakes McCullum to enter New Zealand's top four in Test run charts
briefs.deck: Tom Latham recently surpassed Brendon McCullum as New Zealand's fourth-highest run-scorer in Test cricket. This milestone occurred during the second Test against India at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. Latham scored his 32nd Test half-century during the match, further showcasing his abilities as a player. Kane Williamson continues to hold the record for the most runs for New Zealand in Tests.
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand captain 
Tom Latham
 added another milestone to his Test career on Friday, moving past 
Brendon McCullum
 to become the country's fourth-highest run-scorer in the longest format.
Latham achieved the feat during the opening day's play of the second Test against India at Hagley Oval in Christchurch. The left-handed batter went past McCullum's tally of 6,453 runs, taking his career total to 6,454 in 174 innings across 97 Tests.
McCullum represented New Zealand in 101 Tests between 2004 and 2016, accumulating 6,510 runs in 174 innings. Latham needed just four runs to move ahead of the former captain but had to wait after failing to score in either innings of the series opener at the Basin Reserve in Wellington.
He finally got off the mark in Christchurch on the second ball he faced and moved to 4 runs off nine deliveries on the third ball of New Zealand's third over, crossing McCullum's mark in the process.
Latham also brought up his 32nd Test half-century during the second Test, adding another significant achievement to his day.
The New Zealand captain went on to score 59 off 128 deliveries, hitting six boundaries before Akash Deep brought his innings to an end in the 42nd over. The Indian pacer produced a superb delivery that angled in before holding its line outside off, drawing Latham forward in defence and inducing a fine outside edge. Rishabh Pant completed a straightforward catch behind the stumps to give India a much-needed breakthrough.
Former New Zealand captain 
Kane Williamson
 remains at the top of the all-time list with 9,515 runs from 110 Tests. Williamson, who announced his retirement from Test cricket earlier this year, is followed by Ross Taylor (7,683) and Stephen Fleming (7,172).

briefs.headline: 'We are talking about Siraj, but what about Jadeja?': Gavaskar on India's Test selection
briefs.deck: Sunil Gavaskar expressed concerns regarding India's choice to leave out Ravindra Jadeja for the second Test. He pointed out that Jadeja is a successful bowler in the current World Test Championship cycle. While discussing team selection, Gavaskar also acknowledged the exclusion of pacer Mohammed Siraj from the playing XI. India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and chose to bowl first at Hagley…
briefs.bodyText:
Former India captain 
Sunil Gavaskar
 has questioned India's decision to leave out 
Ravindra Jadeja
 for the second Test against New Zealand in Christchurch. He felt the experienced all-rounder's bowling could have been useful on a pitch that is expected to offer little help to spinners.
India's team selection has sparked a debate, with pacer 
Mohammed Siraj
 also missing out on the playing XI. However, Gavaskar felt Jadeja's omission deserved equal attention.
Speaking on Sony Sports Network after the toss, Gavaskar pointed out that Jadeja has been one of India's most successful bowlers in the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle. He also said the left-arm spinner could have made an impact on the fourth and fifth days of the Test.
"Well, we are only talking about Siraj, but what about Jadeja? He is India's third-highest wicket-taker in this WTC cycle. I do believe his spin would've been pretty useful on the fourth and fifth days. He is someone who is known to grip and turn the ball on placid pitches. So, tough luck for him as well as Mohammed Siraj," said Gavaskar.
Gavaskar on India's playing XI
Despite raising questions over Jadeja's exclusion, Gavaskar backed the team picked by the management. 
He said that once the playing XI is announced, everyone should support the team and hope for a good performance.
"Siraj is the top wicket-taker in this cycle, but let's wait and see. I have always seen it this way: whatever reservations you might have regarding the final XI, 14, or 16, once the team is selected, it is your team and mine. It is the Indian team, after all. So, I am backing this team, and I am praying that this team does well," he added.
Gurnoor Brar makes Test debut
Meanwhile, India captain Shubman Gill won the toss and elected to bowl first in the second Test against New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch.
India made one change to their playing XI, handing a Test debut to pacer Gurnoor Brar. The 26-year-old replaced Prasidh Krishna after the first Test in Wellington ended in a draw.
New Zealand, on the other hand, decided to go with the same playing XI for the series-deciding match.

briefs.headline: 'Deny until you die': Ben Stokes makes explosive remark on Sandpapergate
briefs.deck: With the Sandpapergate controversy dragging on, Ben Stokes has urged for its resolution, noting the strain it has placed on players and their families. He took aim at the Cricket Australia leadership for their poor handling of the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. The recent revelations from Usman Khawaja's memoir have reignited discussions about responsibility and have prompted further reflection on…
briefs.bodyText:
Former England captain 
Ben Stokes
 has urged those involved in the renewed Sandpapergate controversy to bring the matter to a close, warning that the continuing revelations are taking a toll on players, support staff and their families.
Speaking at the launch of his podcast, 
That's Not Cricket
, Stokes said the prolonged public debate was creating unnecessary stress and anxiety for people who had already been through a difficult episode.
While calling for an end to the controversy, Stokes also held the Cricket Australia leadership of the time accountable for the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, saying those in charge "have a lot to answer for". He described the latest developments as a "deny until you die" saga and suggested that the full truth may not emerge anytime soon, given how deeply the issue has become embedded.
"For the sake of players, the staff, the management who were involved in this whole situation, for the sake of their families, for the sake of their friends, the best thing for it to do now would be for it just to stop," he said on his 
That's Not Cricket
 podcast.
Stokes also drew a parallel with his own experience of being under intense media scrutiny, explaining how such situations can affect people beyond those directly involved.
"It’s affecting people who do not deserve to be affected by this. Because I’ve been through something like this when you are so heavily in the media for something, I’ve seen what it’s done to people who don’t deserve to be put through stress, put through anxiety," he added.
However, Stokes was equally critical of Cricket Australia's leadership during the original scandal, questioning the way the episode had been handled and the continued uncertainty surrounding it.
“Whoever was in charge of Cricket Australia at the time has a lot to answer for this. It’s got so deep into it...that it’s almost just like ‘deny until you die’ one way or the other. I’ve been in the dressing room for long enough to form my own very well-educated guess on what I think has happened, but I don’t think in the close future we're going to hear what truly happened because it’s just so deep," he noted.
The Sandpapergate debate has resurfaced nearly eight years after the infamous ball-tampering incident during the 2018 Cape Town Test. Fresh claims by former Australia opener 
Usman Khawaja
 in his memoir have brought the episode back into the spotlight, with the cricketer alleging that the entire team was aware of the ball-tampering plan.
Khawaja's account has reportedly divided opinion within the Australian cricket fraternity and prompted fresh scrutiny of the original investigation, particularly regarding how extensively the incident was examined.
The discussion has since widened, with several current and former cricketers weighing in on Khawaja's claims. His suggestion that Cape Town was not the only Test in which Australia tampered with the ball has further fuelled the controversy.
With fresh accounts continuing to emerge, Stokes believes the renewed debate is now taking a human toll on those connected to the episode and has called for the matter to finally be put to rest.

briefs.headline: Standing up to 140kph: How keepers are turning an old tactic into an attacking weapon
briefs.deck: Wicketkeepers are adapting to modern batting techniques by standing up to fast bowlers in a test match. This tactic aims to restrict the batter's movement and counter advances. Various players like Tom Blundell and Rishabh Pant demonstrate this method effectively in recent games. Former India wicketkeeper Chandrakant Pandit emphasizes the courage required for this approach. Enhanced protective…
briefs.bodyText:
From Alex Carey standing up to Scott Boland in the Ashes to 
Tom Blundell
 doing it against Matt Henry in England and at the Basin Reserve last week and 
Rishabh Pant
 employing the ploy in the first Test, wicketkeepers are increasingly prepared to stand up even when the ball is arriving at 130-140kph.
Beyond the obvious courage required, the keeper is increasingly becoming a thief of the batter’s space.
Former India wicketkeeper 
Chandrakant Pandit
 believes it is a response to how batting has evolved in the post-T20 era. “Today’s batters, even in Tests, have the courage to step out against pace. There is no fear about coming out of the crease to counter movement,” Pandit told TOI from Mohali, where he is coaching Madhya Pradesh in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy.
“So the keeper standing up is basically an attempt to counter that and prevent the batter from advancing.”
There is evidence that it works. Data from New Zealand’s 2026 series in England showed England averaging 25.36 against pace with Blundell back, but only 15.26 when he stood up.
Henry explained why the Kiwis did it at the Basin for a long period of time. “The only mode of dismissal at the Basin was to bring the wickets into play and be prepared to look boring. 
Putting the ball outside off wasn’t going to help as there wasn’t a lot of carry.”
India bowling coach Morne Morkel, though, remains unconvinced. “I’m old school. I like a bit of pace and bounce, balls carrying through to second and third slip, and getting your dismissals that way,” he said on Thursday.
Pandit feels if a batter stands a yard outside his crease, he can alter the length at which the bowler wants to operate.
“When the bowler alters his length, he can also compromise his swing,” he said. “If the wicketkeeper comes up, it puts the batter in two minds. He may want to play a delivery on the front foot, but with the keeper standing up, he might instead play it off the back foot.”
That hesitation can bring bowled and lbw into play without the keeper ever touching the ball.
At The Oval, Blundell stood up for most of Henry’s 24 overs despite the seamer operating around 135kph. All five wickets in Henry’s first-innings five-for came with Blundell up.
For Pandit, that deserves admiration. “The wicketkeeper has to have a lot of courage to stand up at this sort of pace. It means he believes in his skills and is fearless.”
Better protective equipment has helped. “You have helmets now. I don’t remember us wearing helmets while keeping, even on turning tracks or bad wickets. The quality of protective equipment is much better today. But equipment alone cannot give you courage. You still have to believe you can do it.”
Pandit remembers Sunil Gavaskar once asking him to stand up to Raju Kulkarni in domestic cricket. “I started sweating,” he laughs. Gavaskar, he says, was employing some reverse psychology, possibly trying to suggest to the quick that he wasn’t bowling fast enough. Ramakant Desai would also ask Pandit to stand up in club cricket, hoping to create leg-side stumping opportunities off his inswingers.
The tactic carries obvious risks: less reaction time and the possibility of conceding byes. But Pandit believes teams will accept the trade-off. “The idea is to disturb the batter. Tactically, you take that chance.”
Learning the skill, however, requires sustained drills.
“I would start with a tennis ball, hit with a racket from eight or 10 yards so the keeper can work on his reflexes,” he said. “The first thing is to get the fear out of his mind. Then progress to a hard ball with somebody throwing, and after that the bowling machine.”
And repetition counts more than reputation.
“No matter how good you are, you still need to practise. If Rishabh Pant is going to stand close to the stumps, he would definitely have practised it.”

briefs.headline: Streak broken! Siraj's six-year run comes to an end as India drop him again
briefs.deck: Mohammed Siraj's impressive run of playing in all away Test series has come to a halt as he was not selected for the playing XI. Since his introduction to the team in 2020, he had always been a part of these matches until now. With Jasprit Bumrah and other key bowlers back, the selectors chose to include Gurnoor Brar, who is making his Test debut.
briefs.bodyText:
Mohammed Siraj
's remarkable run of featuring in every full away Test series since his debut has finally come to an end, with India leaving the pacer out of their playing XI for the second Test against New Zealand in Christchurch.
Since making his Test debut at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) in 2020, Siraj had never missed an entire away Test series. However, with the team management once again opting against his inclusion for the Christchurch Test, the India pacer will miss his first full away series.
Siraj's omission has attracted considerable attention, particularly given his impressive record in the ongoing World Test Championship (WTC) cycle. The 32-year-old is India's leading wicket-taker in the current cycle, with 43 wickets from 11 matches.
His absence comes after India's bowling attack struggled to force a result in the opening Test at Wellington. Despite putting New Zealand under pressure for large parts of the contest, India could not bowl out the hosts in their second innings, with the match eventually ending in a draw.
Siraj had also been in impressive form, particularly in overseas conditions. 
He played a memorable role in India's dramatic six-run victory over England in the Oval Test last year. The pacer has also been effective in Asian conditions, claiming 21 wickets in seven Tests at an impressive average of 21.28, including a four-wicket haul.
For the opening Test, India had gone in with 
Jasprit Bumrah
, Prasidh Krishna, Akash Deep and Anshul Kamboj as their four specialist fast bowlers, with Washington Sundar providing an additional bowling option. The combination was retained for the second Test, with young pacer Gurnoor Brar replacing Prasidh Krishna and receiving his maiden Test cap.
Siraj is not the only senior player to miss out, with 
Ravindra Jadeja
 also left out of the playing XI for the second consecutive Test. India have continued to back Washington Sundar.
With the two-match series still level at 0-0, India will hope the new-look bowling combination delivers in Christchurch. For Siraj, however, the selection call brings an end to a remarkable streak that had lasted nearly six years.

briefs.headline: Clashes at Besiktas match against Israeli club spark diplomatic row
briefs.deck: Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns
briefs.bodyText:
Istanbul club Besiktas's supporters unfurled a pro-Palestinian banner during a UEFA Europa League match against Israeli side Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia on Thursday (November 26, 2026), prompting a police response and sparking a diplomatic incident that led Turkey's foreign minister to contact his Georgian counterpart.
Also read | Irish athletes’ group urges national team to boycott Israel fixtures
Turkish football fans clashed with police in Batumi, temporarily halting the match, which had been moved from Istanbul over security concerns.
Images from the stadium showed Besiktas supporters displaying a banner reading "Revolt against the occupation, freedom for Palestine", waving Palestinian flags and chanting anti-Israel slogans before police intervened.
Georgia's Interior Ministry said in a statement that "three officers sustained various injuries as a result of the fans' violent actions", adding that 16 people had been detained.
It said some supporters had hurled stadium seats at officers and denied reports that police had used force in response to the display of pro-Palestinian flags and banners.
"We categorically deny these reports and emphasise that the fans' violent actions and physical clashes with police began before the flags and banners were displayed, while they were still marching towards the stadium," the Ministry added.
Police used pepper spray against fans, some of whom required medical attention, Turkey's private DHA news agency reported.
The match was suspended in the 26th minute because of disturbances in the stands, with Danish referee Morten Krogh sending both teams to the dressing rooms.
Turkey's football federation strongly condemned what it described as the "unacceptable" conduct of Georgian police towards Besiktas supporters.
"We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, behaviour and actions directed at Besiktas supporters inside and outside the stadium before and during the UEFA Europa League match," the federation said in a statement.
‘Disproportionate use of force’
UEFA announced last month that the fixture would be moved to Georgia after Turkish authorities informed European football's governing body that, "for safety and security reasons", the match could not be hosted in Istanbul.
Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply since the outbreak of the Gaza war.
President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch supporter of the Palestinian cause, has repeatedly accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza.
Pro-Palestinian banners and chants are seen or heard frequently at Turkish football matches, particularly since the start of the war.
Besiktas said they had lodged a complaint with UEFA over what they described as the "disproportionate" use of force by Georgian police.
"We have launched initiatives with our consulate general in Batumi and UEFA regarding the disproportionate use of force against our supporters by security forces," the club said.
Besiktas added that they would closely monitor the situation until all of their supporters had returned safely to Turkey.
Mr. Erdogan spoke by phone with Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali and said he was closely following developments, the club said.
Messages of support
After the match, which finished 2-1 to Besiktas, Hapoel Beer-Sheva posted a message on social media directed to their travelling supporters.
"Please act responsibly, show restraint and use your best judgement as you leave the stadium and make your way to your accommodation. Follow the instructions of the Georgian security forces, who are responsible for ensuring your safety," the club posted in Hebrew on X.
Messages of support poured in on social media from across Turkey, including from the Sports Minister and Ankara mayor.
Even Besiktas's traditional Istanbul rivals, Galatasaray and Fenerbahce, as well as Black Sea club Trabzonspor, condemned the incidents and expressed solidarity with the club.
A Besiktas club employee told AFP that five supporters were receiving treatment in hospital.
Besiktas supporters scuffled with police and hurled objects at officers as they attempted to make arrests, according to live television footage.
The incidents prompted Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan to call his Georgian counterpart, Maka Botchorishvili.
"Officials from the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate general in Batumi are at the stadium," a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
"All necessary steps are being taken to ensure the safety of our citizens and protect their rights."
